The articles I have read on this seem to be pushing something different -- the old "the science is in and fracking is safe" line.

But, as you noted, there are some serious concerns.

  1. Assuming that fracking regulations actually work to prevent danger, will there be a wave of deregulation later? I'd say most definitely, yes. So fracking will never be "safe" per se.

  2. What is the fair balancing of "fairly low" fracking contamination with drinking water needs? As fracking breaks up more earth, does the risk increase geometrically?

  3. Is the entire system of disposal prone to "spillage"?

  4. If a well-known fracking danger consideration is missing from the report, how can we trust the report to include all the other dangers?

I still have a hard time swallowing this.

What sets this apart from other science issues like GMOs and vaccinations is -- this issue involves greater planetary considerations such as global warming and peak energy. For these reasons, fracking needs to be more than just regulated -- it needs to be minimized or eliminated.

  3. Currently, about 1-3%-ish ends up as spillage. It's totally safe for 97-99% of the sites. /s
  4. This report was ONLY for the safety of the water table. It does NOT address other environmental concerns.

Numbers:

9.4 Million people live within one mile of U.S. fracking locations.

25,000-30,000 new wells were drilled between 2011 and 2014.

There are 6,800 public drinking sources that overlap fracking sites.

Fracking used 44 billion gallons of water per year, which is about 1% of the local water table in most instances.

Spill estimates, depending on the area, range between 0.4% and 12.2%

Calculating spillage estimates and total populations, we have between 37,600 and 1,146,800 people were in spillage affected areas.

Something I'd like to make note of is that many of these areas are generally low income with no other source of revenue other than fracking. It is possible that the numbers are skewed because of areas hiding data. I may have not read deeply enough into how the research was taken, but this looks like a paper report with limited on the ground testing and investigation. This would mean the report could be easily skewed not by the fracking companies, but by the reporting that has been done by the local populace.
It looks like, as we dig deeper and analyze more, we find more problems with the report. Thanks for following-up.
